item.research_question: How can the exploration of the enormous number of High Entropy Alloy (HEA) and Complex Concentrated Alloy (CCA) compositions and their microstructures be accelerated to match the explosion in new alloy bases, and what fundamental data is missing to enable predictive modeling?
item.material_system: High entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), originally defined as blends of 5 or more elements with concentrations between 5 and 35 atom percent, now including systems with as few as 3 principal elements and maximum concentrations higher than 35 atom percent; specific examples mentioned include CoCrFeMnNi, CoCrNi, and Al1.3CoCrCuFeNi.
key_findings: The number of HEA systems with 3 to 6 principal elements from a palette of 75 stable elements exceeds 219 million unique systems.
A 5-component system can have 906 different CCA bases if every 10% change in composition gives a distinct base, leading to over 592 billion new CCA bases.
Refractory metal CCAs (RCCAs) exhibit parabolic oxidation kinetics that are two orders of magnitude lower than conventional refractory alloys.
High entropy alloys show exceptional strength, ductility, and fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures.
The field has explored only seven new alloy families in nearly 15 years, representing a 'linear thinking' approach based on similar atoms.
Current CALPHAD methods cannot predict the presence of ordered B2 intermetallic precipitates in RCCAs because the phase is absent in binary phase diagrams involving refractory metals.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the traditional 'lightly-alloyed-base-element' approach is reaching limits due to a lack of new base elements, whereas HEAs utilize the unexplored central regions of multi-element phase diagrams where all elements are concentrated without a dominant base, creating a vast number of new alloy bases and enabling new physical phenomena such as magnetic hardening and self-healing irradiation resistance.
item.limitations: Exploration must accelerate by 6–9 orders of magnitude to match the explosion in new alloy bases; current scientific efforts rely on data collected more than 50 years ago which is limited to single dominant solvent materials; high throughput tests bring a higher degree of uncertainty; and the field has barely scratched the surface by focusing on only seven new alloy families based on similar atoms.
item.future_work: New high throughput experiments are needed for structural materials; new strategies are needed to navigate the path between composition-dependent and microstructure-dependent properties; acquiring new fundamental data (thermodynamic, phase equilibria, diffusion, etc.) is essential; and the scope of CCA studies must expand to include broader ranges of compositions and uncommon element groupings rather than just equiatomic or near-equiatomic compositions.
quotes: Exploration must accelerate by 6–9 orders of magnitude to match the explosion in new alloy bases.

We need to explore a broader range of compositions in promising alloy systems.
